title: Remembering well
hookLine: yahrzeit candles, stories, and giving in someone's name
tomorrow: Noa's roommate form asks what she believes. where does she start?

cards: Some families keep a voicemail they'll never delete, or a recipe card in a grandmother's handwriting. Jewish families keep a date.
Each year on the anniversary of a death, by the Hebrew calendar, a candle burns through the day. That's the yahrzeit.
And on that same day, in some synagogues, a family brings cake and a bottle after morning prayers and says l'chaim. To life. So which is it, somber or sweet?

teach.h: THE SPIRIT OF MAN IS THE LAMP.
teach.b: Both, and the tradition lets the two views speak.

teach.h: ONE VIEW: A SOLEMN, QUIET DAY.
teach.b: The first says the day is solemn. Proverbs says "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD," and tradition hears the yahrzeit candle in that line: a small flame for a whole life.
The Shulchan Aruch records a custom of fasting on a parent's yahrzeit. Its strongest case: sorrow deserves its own day, unhurried, and a quiet flame keeps faith with it.
The second view says the day is for the life, not only the loss. In Hasidic communities, a great teacher's yahrzeit is kept as a celebration, with songs and stories.

teach.h: THE OTHER: A LIFE WORTH TOASTING.
teach.b: Its strongest case: a life worth mourning is worth toasting, and joy is a way of remembering too. Under both sits one verse: "The memory of the righteous shall be for a blessing."
That's why Jews say of blessed memory after a name.

teach.h: BOTH: KADDISH, A STORY, A GIFT.
teach.b: And both sides do the same three things: say Kaddish, tell a story, give tzedakah in the person's name.
Memory turns into something someone else can use.

how: On a yahrzeit, Jewish families often light a candle that burns through the day, the mourner says Kaddish, and people give tzedakah in the person's memory; some bring food and drink to synagogue for a l'chaim.

o: holding on to sorrow so you never forget
visiting the grave once a year, no more
keeping a memory alive so it blesses others

p: the spirit of man is the lamp
the memory of the righteous, a blessing

games.q: your family's first yahrzeit for your uncle. your aunt wants a quiet candle and Kaddish. your cousin wants his favorite songs and a l'chaim. what's the strongest case for your cousin's side?
o: a life worth mourning is worth toasting; joy remembers too.
candles are old-fashioned, and nobody really needs them now.
after a year, the sadness ought to be over and done.
games.why: both are lived Jewish customs. the candle honors the sorrow; the l'chaim honors the life. and both families say Kaddish, tell a story, and give in his name.

practice: Choose one person you miss. Set a coin aside, or give a few dollars somewhere they'd have cared about, and say their name as you do it. If no one comes to mind, give in the name of someone whose story was told to you.

wordCard.voice: Remembering well: keeping a memory so that it blesses someone, with a candle, a story, Kaddish, or a gift in their name.

orig.note: Hebrew: his memory for a blessing, echoing Proverbs 10:7.

carryVoice: The line to carry: remember well, so the memory becomes a blessing. Until tomorrow, then.
